title: Webb Inspects the Heart of the Phantom Galaxy
caption: The center of the Phantom Galaxy (M74), imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: M 74, Messier 74, NGC 628 · constellation Pisces · about 32 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, J. Lee and the PHANGS-JWST Team. Acknowledgement: J. Schmidt

recognition.text: Ranked #5 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Delicate filaments of gas and dust trace the grand spiral arms that wind outward from the center of this Webb view. This is the heart of M74, the Phantom Galaxy, around 32 million light-years away in Pisces, seen with Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument. With little gas in the nuclear region, Webb has a clear view of the star cluster at the very center.

M74 is a grand design spiral, meaning its arms are prominent and well defined rather than patchy and ragged. It also lies almost face-on to Earth. Together, these traits make it a favorite for astronomers studying how spiral structure arises.

Webb observed M74 to learn about the earliest phases of star formation nearby, as part of the PHANGS collaboration's effort to chart 19 nearby star-forming galaxies in infrared light. Webb's longer wavelengths help pinpoint star-forming regions, gauge how massive and how old star clusters are, and study tiny grains of interstellar dust.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.66 x 2.09 arcminutes) and distance (32 million light years), the frame spans roughly 34,000 × 19,000 light-years. Its light set out about 32 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument observed in mid-infrared light, with the shortest filter shown in blue, then cyan and orange, and the longest in red.
understand.eye: Mid-infrared light is invisible to the human eye.

explore: Hubble had already revealed especially bright star-forming areas in M74 called HII regions. Hubble's sharp ultraviolet and visible view, Webb's infrared sensitivity and radio data from ALMA complement one another. MIRI was contributed by ESA and NASA and built by a European consortium working with JPL and the University of Arizona.
alt: The center of a face-on spiral galaxy, with delicate filaments of gas and dust winding outward in spiral arms around a central star cluster.
